t: How To Regain Calm When You're Feeling Stressed Out https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/09/30/how-to-regain-calm-when-youre-feeling-stressed/
q: The problem with this approach, however, is that it’s unpredictable. It doesn’t always work well or very quickly and, too often, thoughts alone aren’t strong enough to overcome the physical symptoms of stress.

The simplest and most effective method I’ve found to do this is called box breathing. The way it works is that as soon as you start feeling stressed, begin counting to four during each of four phases of breathing.
It’s important to note that when you first try box breathing it can take a little while to get the hang of it. It’s common to inhale too deeply and not exhale quite enough.
The US Navy Seals practice box breathing in order to train the body (and mind) not to go into fight-or-flight mode despite ever-present danger swirling around them.
So the next time you’re feeling stressed-out and anxious, the next time difficult students or time constraints start affecting your peace of mind, commence box breathing.
x: Positive self-talk alone is often insufficient to overcome stress because the body's fight-or-flight response is physically powerful and can contradict what the mind is telling itself.
Box breathing — inhale for four counts, hold for four, exhale for four, hold for four — is a simple, fast technique to interrupt physical stress symptoms.

t: When To Enforce A Consequence And When To Redo A Routine
q: It is one of the most common questions we get here at SCM: “When do I enforce a consequence and when do I redo a routine?
You see, when students fail to perform a routine as taught, in the vast majority of cases it’s either just a small number of students off track or it’s most of the class.
In other words, it’s very rarely in the mid-range of say, 6 to 15 students. So the rule is if it’s just a few, or less, then you enforce individual consequences.
Because, if most of your class is performing a routine incorrectly, then it’s a sign that you may need to reteach the routine in greater detail.
If, on the other hand, the class was disruptive and chaotic, then it's best to stop everything and reteach the routine as if it's the first time.

So the solution is to teach, model, and practice the routine in explicit detail. Raise the bar even higher than it was before, and teach with a passion that refuses to accept anything less than excellence.
x: If only a few students misbehave during a routine, enforce individual consequences for those students specifically.
Off-track routine behavior tends to naturally fall into two patterns — a small number of students, or most of the class — rarely a middling range.
If only a few students misbehave during a routine, enforce individual consequences for those students specifically.
If most of the class is disruptive and chaotic during a routine, stop and reteach it in full detail, since this signals the routine was not adequately taught.

t: Why Your Students Need To Play
q: But the truth is, there is no magic in the classroom management plan itself. The magic is in making it meaningful to your students.
One of the easiest and most rewarding ways to accomplish this is to include more opportunities for play.

Play develops creativity more effectively than any other teaching method. It improves emotional, cognitive, and physical health and teaches students how to be curious self-starters and tenacious problem-solvers.

It readily pulls students into a state of flow, which is proven to be among the most pleasurable human experiences—where time distorts, awareness heightens, and engrossment becomes so intense that they get lost in the moment.

Done right, and within a classroom with clearly defined and faithfully defended boundaries, it can allow you to ask virtually anything of your class—polite behavior, rapt attentiveness, perfect routines—and get it.
Short periods of play sprinkled here and there go a long way toward providing that certain esprit de corps.
x: Rules and consequences alone are only a small part of effective classroom management; the real leverage comes from making the classroom a place students genuinely love being in.

t: The Biggest Reason You Struggle With Consistency stency/
q: But there is one reason that stands out among the rest. It’s a reason that may have never crossed your mind but is responsible for the majority of teachers who struggle with consistency. It’s awkwardness.
The key is to rely on a system that removes the awkwardness and makes your response to misbehavior automatic. Something you no longer have to think about.
Including any more than that risks causing resentment, an awkward interaction, and greater resistance going forward. It also weakens the effect of the consequence.
It’s best to think of yourself as a referee officiating a game. A student breaks a rule and you call a foul. There is no hesitation or time to waver.
Before your students arrive for the day, close your classroom door, position yourself in front of your room, and visualize your most common misbehaviors.
Practice a few more times, visualizing different behaviors. Just follow the script. And later that day, when a student breaks a rule, you’ll find yourself gliding over without a second thought.
x: The primary reason teachers struggle with consistency isn't distraction or unclear rules — it's the simple discomfort, or awkwardness, of confronting a student.

t: How To Handle Unfair Criticism And Turn It Into Your Advantage
q: At some point, unfair criticism happens to everybody. Especially if you’re a newer teacher or new to a school and have yet to establish your reputation.
Those moments when the boss walks in at just the wrong time, or the long months when no one knows who you are, what you stand for, or the excellent work you're doing, don't matter.
Because unfair criticism keeps you on your toes. It forges your determination and mental toughness. It produces even greater excellence.

You see, if instead of worrying over something you have no control over, or worse, trying to explain yourself—which often backfires—you put your head down and stay the course, then your true reputation will reveal itself to everyone on campus.
When I was a new teacher, my principal would leave notes of praise and encouragement in my mailbox.
Let it inspire you to be the mentor, the encourager, and the leader that newer, quieter, or underestimated colleagues aren’t getting from anyone else.
x: Unfair criticism — misjudged moments, out-of-context observations, untrue rumors — happens to nearly every teacher, especially those newer to a school.
